section.title: The Testing of Job
section.sectionRationale: This is the prose prologue that sets the terms for the whole book. Before a single friend opens his mouth, the narrator and the reader are let in on a scene Job never sees: a council in heaven where an accuser questions whether Job's faith is worth anything at all. Everything the dialogue will later thrash out is already decided here, in a conversation Job cannot hear.
section.thesis: Job's uprightness is real, yet Satan accuses it of being bought loyalty, faith for profit; God permits a devastating test to answer the accusation, and in the wreckage of everything he has, Job worships and refuses to charge God with wrongdoing.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: Job's blameless life and careful household piety; the council in heaven where Satan questions Job's motives; the fourfold disaster that strips Job of servants, flocks, and children in a single day; and Job's worship in the ashes.

units.label: Job's blameless life
units.note: a man who feared God and shunned evil

verses.text: There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. And this man was {{tam|blameless}} and upright, {{yare|fearing}} God and shunning evil.
He had seven sons and three daughters,
and he owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 female donkeys, and a very large number of servants. Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East.
Job's sons would take turns holding feasts in their homes, and they would invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

And when the days of feasting were over, Job would send for his children to purify them, rising early in the morning to offer burnt offerings for all of them. For Job thought, "Perhaps my children have sinned and {{barak|cursed}} God in their hearts." This was Job's regular practice.

units.label: The council in heaven
units.note: does Job fear God for nothing

verses.text: One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and {{satan|Satan}} also came with them.

"Where have you come from?" said the LORD to Satan. 
"From roaming through the earth," he replied, "and walking back and forth in it."
Then the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is {{tam|blameless}} and upright, who fears God and shuns evil."
Satan answered the LORD, "Does Job fear God for nothing?
Have You not placed a hedge on every side around him and his household and all that he owns? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.
But stretch out Your hand and strike all that he has, and he will surely {{barak|curse}} You to Your face."

"Very well," said the LORD to Satan. "Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself." 
Then Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.

units.label: The fourfold disaster
units.note: and I alone have escaped to tell you

verses.text: One day, while Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,
a messenger came and reported to Job: "While the oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing nearby,
the Sabeans swooped down and took them away. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you!"
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported: "The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants, and I alone have escaped to tell you!"

While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported: "The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels, and took them away. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you!"
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported: "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,
when suddenly a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you!"

units.label: Job worships
units.note: the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away

verses.text: Then Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped,

saying: 
"Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. {{barak|Blessed}} be the name of the LORD."
In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.

tam.gloss: Blameless, complete, having integrity. It does not mean sinless perfection but a whole, undivided devotion to God that shows itself consistently in conduct. The narrator states it as plain fact before any test begins, and God Himself repeats the verdict to Satan; Job's coming suffering is never explained as punishment for hidden sin.

yare.gloss: To fear, to stand in reverent awe. Paired with shunning evil, it describes a heart rightly oriented toward God, not cringing terror but the reverence that produces obedience. This is the very fear Satan claims is only a business transaction.

satan.gloss: The accuser or adversary, here appearing with the definite article, so a title or role rather than yet a personal name in the way later Scripture uses it. He functions in the council as a prosecutor testing the sincerity of Job's devotion, and later revelation identifies this figure as the devil, the accuser of the brothers, Revelation 12:10.

barak.gloss: To bless, or, ironically, its opposite. In verses 5 and 11 the word is used as a euphemism for cursing God, too terrible an act for the scribes to write plainly; in verse 21 Job uses the same word without irony, actually blessing the LORD's name in the wreckage of his loss. The one word spans the chapter's whole question: will Job's mouth bless God or curse Him when everything is gone?

basic.context: Job is introduced as a real, exceptionally godly man, blameless, upright, wealthy, and careful to guard his children's hearts before God. Then the scene shifts to a place Job never sees: the heavenly council, where Satan questions whether Job's godliness is genuine or simply the product of a comfortable, hedged-in life. God permits Satan to strip away everything Job owns and every child he has, in a single devastating day, but forbids him to touch Job's body. Job's response is worship in the ashes of his losses: he blesses the name of the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter deliberately shows the reader what Job never sees. That gap is the engine of the whole book: the friends will assume Job's suffering must be explained by hidden sin, but the narrator has already told us the real cause was never Job's sin at all. The chapter does not explain why God permits such testing in general; it simply shows that He does, and that Job's faith proves genuine when it costs him everything.
basic.originalLanguages: Job is tam, blameless, a whole and undivided integrity, not sinlessness. Satan asks if Job fears God, yare, for nothing, implying his reverence is bought loyalty. And the Hebrew word barak, bless, does double duty across the chapter: a fearful euphemism for cursing God in verses 5 and 11, and Job's own sincere blessing of the LORD's name in verse 21. The single word holds the whole test in miniature.
basic.typology: Job's willingness to lose everything and still bless God foreshadows the greater righteous sufferer to come, who was tested to the uttermost and did not sin. The accuser who appears in the heavenly court anticipates the New Testament's fuller unveiling of Satan as the accuser of the brothers, finally silenced at the cross.
basic.christ: Job is an innocent man who suffers though he has done nothing to deserve it, and who does not sin in his response. That pattern anticipates Christ, the only truly innocent sufferer, who endured far greater loss and did not charge God with wrongdoing but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. Where Job's faith is tested and proven, Christ's obedience under trial is perfect and becomes the ground of ours.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over Satan's access to Job; nothing happens outside a boundary God sets. He is also confident in His servant, holding up Job as an example to the accuser before the test even begins. This is not a God indifferent to suffering but One who governs it, even when His reasons are hidden from the one suffering.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 5:8 warns that the devil prowls like a roaring lion; Revelation 12:10 names Satan the accuser of the brothers, thrown down; 1 Timothy 6:7 echoes Job's naked I came, naked I will return; Luke 22:31 to 32 shows Satan asking to sift Peter, with Christ interceding for him.
basic.oneStory: The book opens with a test no one on earth can see, a hidden council that will shape thirty seven chapters of unanswered questions. Job's blessing in the ashes plants the book's central question, whether faith in God can survive when every reason to have faith is stripped away, and it points every reader forward to the one greater sufferer whose faith did not fail.

context.literary:
The prologue is built as a staircase of alternating scenes, earth and heaven, and the reader is the only person who stands on both. Job 1:1-5 is on earth, 1:6-12 in heaven, 1:13-22 on earth, and the pattern repeats in 2:1-10, with the friends arriving in 2:11-13. Nothing said in heaven is ever heard on earth. Job and his friends will argue through thirty-seven chapters of poetry without once being told what the reader has just been shown, and that gap is the engine of the book.

Numbers and formulas give the opening an almost liturgical shape. Job has seven sons and three daughters and owns 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys, figures of wholeness and fullness. His regular rhythm of feast, sacrifice and early rising is stated with the phrase 'this was Job's regular practice,' 1:5, and the disaster arrives on a day when the pattern is at its happiest, with the children eating and drinking at the eldest brother's house, 1:13. The four messengers each end with the same report, 'I alone have escaped to tell you,' and each begins before the last has finished, 'While he was still speaking.' The blows fall in a descending order of nearness: the working animals in the field, the flocks by fire, the camels by raiders, and last and worst the children in the house, the only report that has no explanation of who did it beyond a wind.

The heavenly scenes are matched line for line. The LORD asks where Satan has come from, and Satan gives the same answer in 1:7 and 2:2; the LORD offers the same praise of Job in 1:8 and 2:3; Satan makes a challenge and the LORD sets a limit each time. Only the price rises, from 'all that he has' to 'his flesh and bones.'

The chapter closes with a hinge between prose and poetry. Job's final verse of worship in 1:21 is itself a small poem, in three matched lines, and the narrator's verdict in 1:22 sets the standard against which everything Job says from chapter 3 onward will be measured.
context.historical:
The story is set outside Israel, in the land of Uz, and the book never mentions Israel's law, priesthood or covenant. Uz is known from elsewhere as a region linked with Edom, Lamentations 4:21, and Job is called the greatest of the people of the East, a phrase used elsewhere of eastern peoples, Genesis 29:1 and Judges 6:3. His wealth is counted in animals, he lives to 140, and above all he acts as priest for his own household, offering burnt offerings for his children as Noah did after the flood, Genesis 8:20. All of these fit the patriarchal age in the way the story sets its scene. The date of the book's composition is another matter, and readers have proposed anything from the patriarchal age to the time of the exile. The prologue itself simply invites us to read it as a story of an earlier world with lasting force.

Job belonged to a world that knew the question he is about to face. Other ancient Near Eastern writings, among them a Babylonian poem in which a righteous man tells of his sufferings, wrestle with why the pious suffer. Job is not the only ancient text asking that question, and it enters a conversation already under way.

The disasters have plausible ancient shapes. The Sabeans, a people linked to Sheba, and the Chaldeans, here still a raiding people of the desert and not yet the rulers of Babylon, are the kind of raiding bands whose attacks on herds were a real danger. The 'mighty wind from the desert' is a violent storm off the wilderness, and the text says it struck the house at all four corners.

Behind the scene in heaven is the idea, widely shared in the Old Testament, that the LORD presides over a court of heavenly beings, 1 Kings 22:19-22, Psalm 89:6-7.
context.canonical:
The prologue is quoted and echoed across Scripture in unexpected ways. Ezekiel puts Job alongside Noah and Daniel as one of three righteous men whose righteousness could deliver only themselves, Ezekiel 14:14, which shows that Job was known as a righteous figure in Israel's own tradition. James holds him up as an example of perseverance and then adds the crucial phrase: 'You have heard of Job's perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy,' James 5:11. The rest of the book has not yet been told, but James already reads the prologue in the light of the ending.

The figure of the accuser has a short and revealing biography in the canon. In Zechariah 3:1-2 he stands at the right hand of the high priest Joshua to accuse him and is rebuked by the LORD. In 1 Chronicles 21:1 he rises against Israel and incites David to take a census. In Luke 22:31-32 Satan has asked to sift the disciples like wheat, and Jesus has prayed for Simon's faith. In Revelation 12:10 the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down. Job 1 stands at the head of this line and shows the accuser at his most direct: in the presence of God, with a question about Job's motive.

The theme of testing runs across the Old Testament. God tests Abraham, Genesis 22:1-2, and tests Israel in the wilderness to know what was in their hearts, Deuteronomy 8:2-3. The prologue is a distinctive case because the test is set by a challenge from the accuser and the reader is told the reason. The Psalms, meanwhile, wrestle with the prosperity of the wicked and the trouble of the righteous, Psalm 73:1-3, and Jesus later rejects the belief that disaster proves the victim's sin, Luke 13:1-5 and John 9:1-3, in language that reads like a verdict on the friends before they open their mouths.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer builds the opening so that a reader knows more than any character. Job's friends will argue that suffering follows sin and that Job must confess, and the prologue has shut that door before the argument starts: God Himself has twice said there is no one on earth like Job. The author's first purpose is to prevent the reader from being taken in by the friends' logic, which sounds reasonable and is wrong.

His second purpose is to set the real question. Satan does not ask whether Job is good. He asks whether Job's goodness is free, whether he fears God 'for nothing,' 1:9. That is a question about the kind of relationship God has with His creatures: is it a bargain, or is it a bond? The book is asking whether a human being can love God when the reasons for loving Him are taken away. It is also, therefore, a question about God's worth. If Job cursed Him, the accuser would have shown that God is only served for what He gives.

The third purpose is to model an answer for those who suffer. Job's response in 1:20-22 is worship, honest grief and refusal to accuse God. The author does not say that is the only response, and the rest of the book shows Job crying out and demanding answers. But it holds up worship in loss as the ground on which the harder conversation will be held.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes an event in heaven and a sequence of disasters on earth. It does not tell us that every believer's suffering is a wager between God and Satan, and treating it that way would be cruel. Jesus warns against reading tragedy as a verdict on the victim's character, Luke 13:1-5, and the book itself ends with God rebuking the friends who did exactly that, Job 42:7. When someone loses a child, the chapter gives no licence for a bystander to say that it is a test.

It also does not prescribe a fixed pattern of grief. Job tears his robe, shaves his head and falls to the ground: mourning and worship together. Later he will curse the day he was born, 3:1, and demand a hearing, and God will say he spoke of Him rightly, 42:7. The chapter permits both the composed worship and the raw protest.

What does carry over as instruction is the shape of the blessing in verse 21. It confesses that everything came as a gift, that the giver has the right to take, and that the name of the LORD is worth blessing whichever He does. It also holds a warning for parents in verse 5: a father who is watchful for his children's spiritual condition, and who brings them to God regularly, is commended by the text and not mocked.

debates.question: Who are the 'sons of God' who present themselves before the LORD in 1:6?

views.label: Heavenly beings, the angelic court
views.case: The phrase is used of heavenly beings in Job 38:7, where the sons of God shout for joy at creation, and the same picture of a heavenly assembly appears in Psalm 89:6-7 and 1 Kings 22:19-22, where the LORD sits on His throne with the host of heaven around Him. This has been the dominant reading in the church from the early centuries, and it fits the scene, in which beings come to present themselves and report on their errands.

views.label: Human worshippers or leaders
views.case: A minority of readers have taken the phrase to describe the righteous on earth, on the ground that the Old Testament sometimes calls Israel God's son. The difficulty is that Satan is said to come 'among' or 'with' them, that they present themselves before the LORD in a heavenly setting, and that Job 38:7 clearly refers to beings who were present at creation.

debates.bearing: The reading of heavenly beings fits the whole book. The point of the scene is not the identity of the assembly but that the whole cosmos, including the accuser, is answerable to the LORD.

debates.question: Who is responsible for the disasters: Satan, the raiders, nature, or God?

views.label: God ordains, and Satan and human agents act within His decree
views.case: Job says 'The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away,' 1:21, and the narrator approves: Job did not sin. In 2:10 he asks whether we should receive adversity from God, and at the end the friends console him for 'all the adversity that the LORD had brought upon him,' 42:11. Calvin and many of the Reformers read the chapter as a strong statement of providence: Satan's power is a leash held by God, and the Sabeans and Chaldeans are real agents whose guilt is their own.

views.label: God permits within limits, and the evil is the accuser's and the raiders'
views.case: The text is careful about who does what. God sets the boundary, 'Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself,' and Satan goes out. The killing is done by Sabeans and Chaldeans, the fire and wind are the elements at work, and Job's own words attribute all of it to the LORD without any hint that God is at fault, 1:22. On this reading God allows what He does not do.

views.label: The text refuses to explain the mechanism
views.case: The narrator gives the scene in heaven and the sequence on earth and stops. The messengers name only human and natural causes. Job names God. The messengers never mention Satan. The book keeps these threads apart on purpose, so that the reader must hold them together without being handed a formula.

debates.bearing: All three agree that God is not the author of Job's guilt, that Job's response is approved, and that the book will not let us settle the question by explaining Job's suffering away.

study.originalLanguages:
The Hebrew of the prologue is full of small words that carry large weight. Start with the accuser. The Hebrew says 'the satan,' with the definite article, in 1:6 and 2:1, so it is a role before it is a name, the one who accuses. The root means to oppose or be an adversary. In Numbers 22:22 the angel of the LORD stands in the road as an adversary to Balaam, using the same root. In 1 Chronicles 21:1 the word appears without the article and is usually read as the name. The book of Job shows the role at the moment before it hardens into a name.

The word 'roaming' in 1:7 is a verb of going to and fro, and its counterpart in Zechariah 1:10-11 describes the beings the LORD sent to patrol the earth. Satan's report, that he has been roaming through the earth, has the shape of the report of a patrol, and it is worth noting that in Zechariah the answer is that all the earth is tranquil.

In 1:8 the LORD asks, 'Have you considered My servant Job?' The literal idiom is 'have you set your heart upon,' the language of close attention. It is God, not Satan, who first raises Job's name. And 'My servant' is a title of honour, the one God gives to Moses in Numbers 12:7, and here it is given to a man with no covenant, no law and no land.

The word for 'for nothing' in 1:9 is chinnam, meaning without cost, without reward, or without cause. The wordplay that follows is deliberate. In 2:3 the LORD says that Satan incited Him against Job to ruin him 'without cause,' and the word in Hebrew is again chinnam. The accuser asks whether Job serves God for nothing, and God answers that it is the accuser who has attacked Job for nothing. The same word is turned on the one who used it.

The 'hedge' in 1:10 is a verb of fencing in, and Job uses the same root in 3:23 when he asks why life is given to a man 'whom God has hedged in.' What Satan calls protection Job will soon experience as a wall around him with no exit. The book lets one word carry both the blessing and the burden.

Satan says 'strike all that he has' in 1:11, but the Hebrew verb means to touch. It is the verb used in 1:19 when the wind 'struck' the four corners of the house, and again in 2:5 when Satan asks to touch his bone and flesh. The idiom of the hand is also worth noting. In 1:11 Satan says 'stretch out Your hand,' and in 1:12 God says he may not 'lay a hand' on the man himself. The phrase to send or stretch out the hand is the same idiom used of an attack, and the limit God sets is worded in the terms of the attack.

Finally, in 1:22 the phrase 'charge God with wrongdoing' uses a rare noun, tiphlah, which describes something tasteless or unseemly. Older English versions render it 'foolishly.' The same noun appears in 24:12, where Job says that God does not charge anyone with wrongdoing.

typology.type: Job the blameless man who suffers and does not sin, Job 1:22
typology.fulfillment: Job is presented as a righteous man who loses everything he has and yet does not accuse God. The correspondence with Christ is real: He was tempted in every way and was without sin, Hebrews 4:15, and 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8. He offered up prayers with loud cries and tears, Hebrews 5:7. Isaiah sees the servant as 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief,' Isaiah 53:3. But the pattern breaks in an important place: Job ends by retracting his words and repenting in dust and ashes, Job 42:6, and Christ has nothing to retract. Job points to Christ by resemblance and by need.

typology.type: The accuser before the throne and the answer to his charge, Job 1:9-11
typology.fulfillment: Satan's charge is that Job's righteousness is not real, and the drama tests it. In Zechariah 3:1-2 the accuser stands at the priest's right hand and is rebuked, and Revelation 12:10-11 says the accuser of our brothers is thrown down because they overcame him 'by the blood of the Lamb.' Job's own answer to accusation was his integrity. The answer of the gospel is that no charge can stand at all: 'Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies,' Romans 8:33. The type falls short because Job had to defend himself, and believers do not.

typology.type: Job the priest of his household, Job 1:5
typology.fulfillment: Job rises early to offer burnt offerings for each of his children, in case they have sinned, and the text says this was his regular practice. It is a picture of intercession, and it points to Christ, who 'always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25. The escalation is stark. Job offered again and again, always with the word 'perhaps.' Christ 'sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself,' Hebrews 7:27. Job could not be sure his sacrifices were enough. Christ's offering is finished, and He also intercedes for the ones He has saved.

typology.type: The LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, Job 1:21
typology.fulfillment: Job receives loss as something taken from him. Jesus in the garden asks that the cup pass and then says 'not My will, but Yours be done,' Luke 22:42, and He tells His disciples, 'No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord,' John 10:18. The pattern is that the righteous submit to the Father in loss. The escalation is that Job's loss was inflicted, while the Son's was freely given, and Job lost a hedge, while Christ was forsaken, Matthew 27:46, and gave His life so that others could be brought in.

study.christ:
The book of Job is not a coded description of Jesus, and its hero is not sinless. But the book leads to Christ in three ways that the New Testament itself confirms.

It leads to Christ by pattern. Job is an innocent man who loses everything and does not sin. The Gospel of Luke tells us that Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness and tempted by the devil, and that when the devil had finished every temptation he left Him until an opportune time, Luke 4:1-13. Like Job, Jesus was declared beloved before the testing, at His baptism, Matthew 3:17, and the tempter's first move was to ask what was true of Him: 'If You are the Son of God,' Matthew 4:3. Like Job, Jesus is hungry, alone and stripped of protection, and answers with the word of God. The whole life of Jesus is a long answer to the accuser's question, whether anyone will fear God for nothing. Hebrews says He 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8, and that He is a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses because He was tempted in every way and did not sin, Hebrews 4:15.

It leads to Christ by contrast. Job's hedge was removed and he did not know why. Jesus, at the cross, cried 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' and gave His life, John 10:18. Job's suffering was not atoning. Christ's is. Job needed an umpire and said so in 9:33, where he says there is no mediator between us. In Christ, God has provided one, and the one who stands between God and the sufferer is the one who suffered. The New Testament says that God made Him 'sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21.

It leads to Christ by the accuser's defeat. Satan's whole method in Job is to charge and to test. The New Testament announces that his accusing days are numbered. Jesus says 'now the prince of this world will be cast out,' John 12:31. Revelation says the accuser has been thrown down, and that believers conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 12:10-11. Paul asks who will bring any charge against God's elect, and answers that Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at the right hand of God interceding for us, Romans 8:33-34. Job 1:5 shows a father interceding at dawn for children who may have sinned; Luke 22:32 shows Jesus praying that Simon's faith would not fail.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Job's suffering does not always mirror ours, and the prologue never claims that we can explain our own suffering as a test. Jesus refuses that kind of reading in John 9:3 and Luke 13:1-5. What the chapter gives is the shape of the problem and the promise that the one Sufferer who has answered the accuser has done so for us.
study.god:
The prologue shows a God who is sovereign in a way that is more surprising than a sentence like 'God is in control' can carry. He is the one who first brings up Job's name. Satan arrives with a report, and it is the LORD who asks, 'Have you considered My servant Job?' The God who is confident in His servant is not passive. He also holds a boundary around the accuser, in 1:12 and again in 2:6. 'Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself.' Satan can do what he does only because he has been given room, and can do no more than he has been given.

The chapter holds together two things that many readers find hard to hold. God permits real evil and does not cause it in the way Satan's raiders or the wind cause it. And God is not aloof: He rules over every one of these events. Job's confession, 'The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away,' has the whole of the Bible's providence behind it. Lamentations asks, 'Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?' Lamentations 3:38, and Isaiah 45:7 has God say He brings prosperity and creates calamity. Yet nothing in the chapter says God is the source of wrong. The book keeps God's sovereignty and God's goodness in the same sentence and refuses to resolve them into a formula.

He is also a God whose worth is the real subject. The accuser's question, 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' is a charge against God as much as against Job. It says that God can be served only for what He pays. The chapter's answer, given in Job's worship, is that God is worth blessing when there is nothing left to be given. That is a claim about the glory of God, and it is why the chapter ends in the word 'blessed.' The one who fears God for nothing has seen that God Himself is the treasure.

He is a God who does not owe an explanation. Job is never told what happened in heaven. When God finally speaks, in chapter 38, He does not explain the test. The book will show that not being told is not the same as being abandoned. God is present in the silence, and at the end He says Job has spoken of Him rightly, Job 42:7. James draws the conclusion that the outcome from the Lord shows Him to be full of compassion and mercy, James 5:11.

For worship, the chapter teaches the shape of a blessing that can be prayed in the dark. Job falls to the ground, and it is an act of worship. He confesses what he was given and what he has lost, and he praises the name of the one who did both. That posture is echoed in Habakkuk 3:17-18, where the fig tree does not bud and yet the prophet will rejoice in the God of his salvation. It is not stoicism. It is the recognition that the giver is greater than the gifts.

crossReferences.note: The second round of the same test. God again praises Job and adds that Satan incited Him against Job 'without cause,' using the same Hebrew word that Satan used for 'for nothing.' Job's wife urges him to curse God and die, and Job asks whether we should accept only good from God, and the narrator says he did not sin in what he said.

Job uses the word for hedge that Satan used in 1:10. What Satan called protection, Job now experiences as confinement. The word ties the prologue to the first speech and shows how one Hebrew root can carry both blessing and burden.

The poem on wisdom says that fearing the Lord is wisdom and turning from evil is understanding, the same pair of terms that describe Job in 1:1 and 1:8. The prologue's description of Job is thus the book's own definition of wisdom.

God vindicates Job and rebukes the three friends, saying they have not spoken of Him accurately as Job has. Job is then told to pray for them and offer burnt offerings, which recalls his priestly role in 1:5. The rebuke confirms what the prologue told the reader from the start.

Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him, and the LORD rebukes him. The scene is another glimpse of the accuser in the heavenly court, and it shows that his accusations do not stand against those the LORD has chosen.

Micaiah sees the LORD on His throne with the host of heaven around Him, and a spirit steps forward and is given permission to entice Ahab. It is a second Old Testament picture of a heavenly council in which a spirit works only with the LORD's permission, and it helps show how the scene in Job 1 fits the wider biblical world.

God tests Abraham by asking him to offer his son, and Abraham obeys. Job 1 and Genesis 22 are the two great Old Testament stories of testing. In both the reader knows that it is a test and the servant does not, and in both the servant answers with obedience and worship.

Jesus tells Simon that Satan has asked to sift the disciples like wheat, and that He has prayed that Simon's faith will not fail. It is the New Testament counterpart to Job 1: an accuser asks for leave, a limit is set, and this time the sufferer is told of the prayer that is holding him.

The dragon, the ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, is thrown down, and the accuser of our brothers is silenced. They conquer him by the blood of the Lamb. This is where Job 1's accuser ends up, and it shows that the accusation of the prologue is finally answered by the cross.

The adversary prowls like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour, and believers are told to resist him, standing firm in faith and knowing that brothers throughout the world suffer the same. The echo of Satan's roaming in Job 1:7 is plain, and so is the reassurance that no believer is suffering alone.

James holds up Job's perseverance and reminds his readers of the outcome from the Lord, who is full of compassion and mercy. It shows how the New Testament reads the prologue: as the beginning of a story that ends in mercy.

The disciples ask who sinned when a man is born blind, and Jesus says neither did, but that the works of God would be displayed in him. It is Jesus' own rejection of the friends' theology, and it reads like a commentary on the Job prologue.

Jesus offered prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears, and although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered. Here is the innocent sufferer that Job foreshadows, and here is the difference: Christ's suffering is obedience that saves.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world in which everything is very good and human beings live in the presence of God in a garden. Job's life in the first five verses looks like a shadow of that world. He is blameless, he is blessed with children and flocks, God has hedged him in, and he acts as priest for his family. Then a voice from outside puts the old question to him: is the relationship real, or is it a bargain? In Genesis 3 the serpent asks 'Did God really say?' and brings the man and woman to doubt God's goodness. In Job 1 the accuser asks whether anyone serves God for nothing and tries to bring Job to the same doubt. Adam failed in a garden of plenty. Job stands in a ruin.

The story goes on to show what the Bible will say again and again: that faith is tested and that the testing is not proof of sin. Abraham is tested, Genesis 22:1. Israel is tested in the wilderness, Deuteronomy 8:2. Jesus is tested in the desert, Matthew 4:1-4. The church is told that the proven character of its faith is more precious than gold, 1 Peter 1:6-7. Job sits at the centre of this line, an outsider to the covenant whose faith is nevertheless real.

The question the prologue asks is finally answered in Christ. He is the Son who fears the Father not for reward but because He is the Son, who gives Himself at the cross, and who, in rising, silences the accuser. Job in the ashes asks for a mediator, Job 9:33, and does not get one. In Christ the Mediator has come, and Job's cry that he knows his Redeemer lives, Job 19:25, is answered by the resurrection.

The church now lives in the time between the accuser's defeat and his removal. He still prowls, 1 Peter 5:8, but he has been thrown down and cannot stand against those Christ intercedes for, Romans 8:33-34. Believers weep, as Job did, and they worship, as Job did, and they wait.

In the new creation the accuser is bound and the whole question is closed, Revelation 20:2. The epilogue of Job's restored family and doubled flocks, Job 42:10-17, is a shadow of what is coming. God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The one who seemed to be taken away in the dust will be seen face to face, and the blessing that began with 'Blessed be the name of the LORD' will be sung without a hint of loss.

sermon.title: Questions of Suffering
sermon.why: Keller works through Job 1:8-22 to show that the book refuses pat answers to suffering, calls believers to embrace living without an explanation, and points forward to the ultimate answer found in Christ, matching this chapter's refusal of easy theology.

quiz.q: What does Satan claim is the real reason for Job's godliness?

options.text: That Job's fear of God is bought loyalty, dependent on God's blessings, and would collapse if they were removed.
options.note: This is exactly Satan's challenge in verses 9 to 11: does Job fear God for nothing.

options.text: That Job only serves God because his life has been comfortable and untested so far.
options.note: Close to Satan's real charge, but less precise than naming it as bought loyalty tied directly to God's blessings.

options.text: That Job is secretly guilty of some hidden sin.
options.note: Satan never accuses Job of sin; his charge is about motive, not hidden guilt, though this confusion anticipates the friends' later argument.

options.text: That Job does not really believe God exists.
options.note: Satan does not question Job's belief, only whether his devotion is self-interested.

quiz.q: What boundary does God place on Satan's test?

options.text: Satan may take everything Job has, but he must not lay a hand on Job himself.
options.note: Verse 12 states this limit precisely; God's sovereignty governs even the scope of the test.

options.text: Satan is given wide freedom to attack Job's possessions and family, but God still keeps him on a leash.
options.note: Captures the general truth of a bounded permission, though less exact than naming the specific limit stated in verse 12.

options.text: Satan may harm Job's body but not take his possessions.
options.note: This reverses the actual boundary set in chapter 1.

options.text: Satan may do anything he likes without restriction.
options.note: The text is explicit that Satan operates only within a limit God sets.

quiz.q: How does the narrator evaluate Job's response to his catastrophic losses?

options.text: In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.
options.note: Verse 22 gives the narrator's own verdict on Job's worship and words.

options.text: Job tore his robe, shaved his head, and wept in grief, but still fell down and worshiped.
options.note: A true description of Job's visible grief, though it stops short of the narrator's explicit verdict that he did not sin.

options.text: Job sinned in his heart but not in his words.
options.note: The text makes no such distinction here; that nuance appears later, after the second test in chapter 2.

options.text: Job cursed God as his wife would later suggest.
options.note: This is the opposite of what happens; Job blesses the LORD's name instead.

quiz.q: Why does the narrator let the reader see the heavenly council when Job himself never learns of it?

options.text: So the reader knows Job's suffering is not caused by his sin, which sharpens the irony when the friends later assume it is.
options.note: This gap between what the reader knows and what Job's friends will assume drives the whole book's tension.

options.text: So the reader can watch the coming debate with more information than any character in the story has.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but less precise than naming the specific irony the council creates against the friends' theology.

options.text: So the reader can conclude that Satan is more powerful than God.
options.note: The council scene shows the opposite: Satan operates only by God's permission and within His limits.

options.text: To prove that Job actually was guilty of secret sin.
options.note: The council scene establishes precisely the opposite: God Himself calls Job blameless.

quiz.q: What does the wordplay on 'bless' (barak) in this chapter reveal?

options.text: The same Hebrew word is used as a fearful euphemism for cursing God, and then, in Job's own mouth, for sincerely blessing Him, holding the whole test in one word.
options.note: Verses 5, 11, and 21 all use barak, moving from feared curse to genuine worship.

options.text: Hebrew sometimes uses a single word to cover both a blessing and its ironic opposite, and this chapter shows that pattern at work.
options.note: True in general, but less precise than identifying the exact movement from feared curse to sincere blessing across verses 5, 11, and 21.

options.text: It shows Job secretly cursed God despite what the narrator says.
options.note: The narrator explicitly states in verse 22 that Job did not sin; his use of bless in verse 21 is sincere worship.

options.text: It proves the text has been mistranslated.
options.note: The euphemistic use of bless for curse is a recognized feature of the Hebrew text, not a translation error.

questions: Job worshiped in the immediate aftermath of catastrophic loss, before he had any explanation. Where do you tend to locate your security, and what would it cost you to still bless God there if it were stripped away?
Satan's accusation was that Job's faith was only as deep as his comfort. Has your own faith ever been tested by loss in a way that exposed what it was really resting on?

The chapter never explains to Job why he suffers, and neither will the rest of the book. How do you sit with unanswered 'why' questions in your own life, without manufacturing an explanation God has not given?
God set a firm boundary that Satan could not cross. Does knowing that evil operates only within God's permission bring you comfort, unease, or both, and why?
The text says Job did not sin in what he said. What would it look like for you to grieve honestly, even angrily, without crossing into accusing God of wrongdoing?

translationNotes.note: Blameless renders the Hebrew tam, describing wholehearted integrity rather than sinless perfection; the same root gives the noun tummah, integrity, that Job's wife will mock in 2:9.
Cursed renders barak, literally bless, used here as a reverent scribal euphemism to avoid writing the word curse next to God's name; the same word is used in its plain sense, sincerely, in verse 21.
The Satan carries the definite article in Hebrew, functioning here as a title, the accuser or adversary, within the heavenly court, rather than simply a personal name.
